01

Where the name comes from

?Is Tinker banned in Commander?

I upgraded my first Commander deck by hand, with cards I'd kept since I was a kid. I put Tinker in it and thought it was awesome. My friends and I played it for months. Then I took it to my local game store and was told, promptly, that Tinker is banned.

Most Commander players have a story like that. Yours might be a judge explaining color identity, or a precon that got eaten on turn four. edh.wtf is named for the question you ask right after.

We don't have all the answers. The people at your table usually have most of them, and so do the players who write here. We take notes, we show where we checked, and we leave the call to you and your pod.

Jaime, who started edh.wtf

What we believe

  • Rules are flat. Taste belongs to the pod.Tinker is banned: we say that plainly. Land counts, tutors, proxies and brackets are choices, and we say what we'd do in the first person.
  • Every note shows where to check it.A card's text, a rule number or a count sits beside every note.
  • Every note is signed.A player who plays the deck signs it.
  • When we're wrong, we say so where you can see it.This house started with a wrong call about Tinker.
  • The name is the only loud thing.Everything else keeps its voice down.
02

The idea

?edh.wtf asks.

The table answers.

The name is the player's question. It is what someone says the first time a precon gets eaten by a turn-four combo, the first time a judge explains color identity, the first time someone at the store says that card is banned. Players say EDH where the publisher's marketing says Commander, so the name is in their words twice.

The answer comes from the table: players who play Commander, writing notes the way a friend marks up your decklist, with where to check each one.

How a loud name stays polite

  • The suffix is never spelled out.Its letters stay in the address and never appear as a word in a sentence.
  • Nothing printed carries it.Goods, labels and packs print edh.how or edh.supply.

The tagline

Notes on your 99. Your call.

It says what we offer (notes), on what (your 99, the cards under your commander) and who decides (you). It holds even for the banned list: your pod can still agree to play Tinker under rule zero.

For EDH Supply goods only. It keeps the lead line's shape: what we offer, then who decides.

Playtest the 99. Your table decides.

Which line leads: when a screen, banner or social card carries one brand line, it is the tagline. The idea explains the brand to the people who make it. Outside this book it appears only on the About page.

One house, three addresses

  • The house, on screens and on the Discord server.
  • The address we print: labels, pack backs, anything on paper, and the one you say out loud in polite company.
  • EDH Supply, the goods line: playtest paper, labels, precons.

Naming

LinePatternExample
ToolsA word players already useMana Base Builder
GuidesThe question, the way players ask itWhy does every deck run Command Tower?
PrintablesThe thing, then a numberDeck Box Labels No. 01

A new name joins the family

A new edh.* name joins as part of the same house: its suffix names the job, its wordmark comes from the same family, and it never becomes a second brand. Pvragon is named once, in the footer: edh.wtf is made by Pvragon.

03

Who it is for

Commander players, and only Commander players. Five people, written from desk research before any interviews, so treat them as a starting point to test.

Theo

The tinkerer, the primary reader

Theo owns a dozen decks, brews something every week and rebuilds one every few weeks. He plays brackets 2 and 3, would rather lose an interesting game than win a boring one, and dislikes tutors.

I don't need to be told the best deck. I need to know why it misses its fourth land drop, and then I'll decide.

Maya

In her first month

Maya bought a precon a few weeks ago and has played three games. She has a list of questions she's embarrassed to ask out loud.

I don't mind being new. I mind being made to feel new.

Jess

Budget, proxy-curious

Jess loves the format, can't justify $40 for a land, and wants to play a card for a month before paying for it.

Just tell me where the line is and let my pod decide the rest.

Priya

The organizer

Priya keeps every deck labeled and every box in its place. She hosts the pod night and lends decks to newcomers.

If it prints crooked the first time, I'm not trying it a second time.

Dan

The precon buyer

Dan buys a few precons a year, for himself, a friend or a kid, and is tired of paying more than the box says at release.

Tell me if it's fun out of the box. I'll figure out the upgrades.

Who it is not for

  • Not aimed at cEDH and tournament grindersYou are welcome to read along. We write for kitchen-table and store-night Commander.
  • Never for speculators and flippersPlayers already blame them for scarcity. Nothing here is written to help them.
04

Where it stands

For Commander players who would rather decide for themselves than be told, and who want to know why their deck does what it does, edh.wtf is a Commander-only home for notes on your 99: each written and signed by a player, each showing where to check it, with taste left to your pod. Unlike EDHREC's popularity data, edh.tools' unsigned reasons, Commander's Herald's opinion columns and Moxfield's one-off primers, every note here is signed, checkable and corrected in public.

The one claim only edh.wtf can make

edh.wtf is the only Commander house where every note is signed by a player, shows where to check it, leaves taste to your pod and gets corrected in public.

Signing and public correction start with the first page, and this line goes into public copy only once they have.

What edh.wtf is not

  • Not a rulingWe explain rules and cite them. A judge rules at an event; your pod rules on rule zero.
  • Not a proxy shopWe never sell printed cards. Playtest paper is blank.
  • Not an AI deck generatorWe write notes on the deck you built.
  • Not the publisherNo mana symbols, card frames or lookalike type.
05

The player in the next seat

Principles

  • 01Ask it the way players ask it.Headlines and guide titles use players' own words, taken from what they search for and the questions they post.
  • 02Talk like the player in the next seat.The first sentence answers. Name the card and give the number. A take comes in the first person, "we run 37", followed by "your pod may like it greedier".
  • 03Show where to check it.Write the citation as an invitation, "see CR 903.4", so a player can check us.
  • 04Sign it, and fix it in public.A guide is one player's notes, so it carries their name. A mistake is fixed where it was made, and the fix stays on the page.
  • 05Dry is allowed; rude is not.Jokes are the kind regulars make at the pod: about Sol Ring, about salt, about the deck that never draws its third land. Never at the player who asked.
  • 06Explain a term the first time it matters.Brand lines use players' words without explaining them. Guides and help use the term, then make it plain in the same sentence.
  • 07The name stays in the address.Write edh.wtf whole, or say the house.
  • 08End with the player or the table.Every line leaves the decision with a player or the pod.

Never

  • Swearing, in any formIn copy, captions, replies and on the Discord server.
  • Know-it-all phrasingThe correct build, you should, always, never, about a pod's choice. Obviously, simply, everyone knows.
  • Hype and scarcityDrop as a release, only N left, countdown, limited time, insane value, must-have. Land drop is fine.
  • Speculator wordsInvestment, ROI, flip, whale.
  • Software-marketing wordsElevate, unlock, unleash, level up, supercharge, seamless, all-in-one, game-changer. The Commander Game Changers list keeps its name.
  • AI in a nameNothing called AI-powered, and no tool called AI anything.
  • Praise of ourselvesFair, honest, trusted, the best.
  • EmojiAnywhere.

Brand lines

Each line names a real card, rule or player word, and ends with a player or the pod deciding. Card facts are rechecked against Scryfall before a line is published; line 03's counts are illustrative.

Notes, for the player in their first month

Guides and help pass the newcomer test: a term is used, then made plain in the same sentence. Every guide is signed. The names below are samples until real writers sign.

?Is Tinker still banned in Commander?

Samplays Kenrith group hug

Yes. Tinker is on the Commander banned list, the short list of cards no Commander deck may include. Your pod, the group you play with, can still agree to allow it in a casual game. That agreement is called rule zero. At a store event, the banned list applies.

In our pod we run Shape Anew for the same idea, without the search. Whether you want either is your pod's call.

CheckCommander banned list

The legal card we run instead:

  • 1Shape AnewTrades an artifact for the next artifact in your library. You get whatever turns up first. Legal, and not a Game Changer.U

Wrong? Tell us and we correct this guide in public, with the date.

?How many lands in an EDH deck?

Samplays Kenrith group hug

Most decks run 36 to 38 lands. An EDH deck, also called a Commander deck, is 100 cards: your commander plus 99 others, which players call the 99.

We run 37 when the 99 has five or more mana rocks, artifacts such as Sol Ring and Arcane Signet that tap for mana, and 38 when our best cards cost 6 or more. Your pod may play it greedier or safer.

Count36 to 38CheckEDHREC land counts

Wrong? Tell us and we correct this guide in public, with the date.

When a pasted list has a typo

Couldn't read one line

We couldn't read line 14, "Sol Rnig". Fix the spelling and paste the list again. Every other line came through.

The Discord server's first rule

No question is too basic. Someone asked it last week, and someone will ask it next week.

Signed, and corrected in public

  • Every guide carries a bylineIt gives a player's name and a deck they play, beside the question.
  • Every guide and tool page asks to be correctedA visible "Wrong? Tell us" sits beside the answer.
  • Corrections stay on the pageEach one is dated and says what was wrong and what changed, with thanks to whoever caught it.

Corrected November 12, 2026

What each color is for

  • Sheet is where you readEvery guide, tool result and page sits on it, like a decklist written out at the table.
  • Top Sheet is a panelIt is the fresh page on top of the pad, a little lighter than Sheet. Tables, specs and mocks sit on it.
  • Ruled is the line on the sheetIt draws the faint rules under each row, the margin and the frame, and never fills a page.
  • Walnut is the kitchen tablePlenty of Commander games happen on one, so keep it warm.
  • The six keys mean Magic colorsThey show each card's real color identity, the same on the sheet and on the table. No other color stands for a Magic color.

Marker and Counter

  • Marker is the flat answerA band behind Ink text, once per view, on the rules fact. It stays off links, buttons, prices and hover states, and never appears on anything we sell.
  • Counter is the player's takeA band behind Ink text on a byline or a first-person note. It stays off prices and buy buttons. A line that hands the call to the table stays in Ink.
  • Links and buttons stay in InkLinks are underlined, and the underline thickens on hover. Focus is an outline in the text color.

Type: the question, the notes, the count

Schibsted Grotesk asks the question. Atkinson Hyperlegible Next writes the notes, which is most of what anyone reads. Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono is kept for counts and rule numbers, so a page never reads as code.

The question: Schibsted Grotesk 800 and 900

Why does every deck run Command Tower?

It sets question rows, edh and headings: 800 for questions, 900 only for edh and the cover. Normal word spacing at every size. Free under the SIL Open Font License.

The notes: Atkinson Hyperlegible Next 400 to 700

It taps for any color in your commander's color identity, and it enters untapped. We run it in every deck with three or more colors.

It sets body text, card names, labels, bylines and buttons. Labels are 700, in sentence case.

The count: Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono 500 to 800

CR 903.4 38 / 100
I l 1 O 0

It sets counts, rule numbers and tag values, on fewer than one line in five on any page. The 99 column is texture, so it is set in the notes face.

09

Mark and wordmarks

Every Magic player turns cards sideways dozens of times a game, so the tap says Magic before anything else does. The table around it and the 99 say Commander.

The drawn master

Our own screens and the Discord server.

The address on anything printed.

EDH Supply, the goods line.

What it shows, and the rules

The mark is two identical solid cards with a real card's proportion. One stands upright. The other is the same card tapped, lying in front across its lower corner with a clear gap of table around it, the way a played card lands.

Each card carries one line where its text box begins, and that line is what says playing card at a glance. In the Walnut tile the line is a mid tone and stops short of the card's edge. A dark line from edge to edge cuts a card into two panes, and the tile then reads as a window.

In a browser tab and as an app icon, the two cards sit on a small Walnut tile, with light faces inside dark borders, the way real cards look on the table.

It carries one idea, the tap. The question lives in the name and in the question row, so the mark doesn't repeat it.

  • Never a buttonThe mark is the logo: header, tab icon, goods. It is never a clickable icon inside a page.
  • Never filled with Marker or CounterThose inks mark notes on the sheet.
  • Keep the card in front and the gapThe tapped card always lies in front, with table showing all round it; in the Walnut tile, its dark border keeps the two cards apart. Both cards keep their text-box line, and in the tile it stays a mid tone that never touches the border. In a wordmark, the mark runs from the top of the h in edh down to the descender line below the baseline.
  • Interim until letteredThese drawings are working versions. The wordmarks stay out of public use until they are lettered.

Minimum sizes

  • Mark on screen, 64 px and upScale the drawn mark freely.
  • Mark below 64 pxUse the pixel fittings at 48, 32 and 24 px, drawn so every edge lands on a whole pixel. In one color, 24 px is the smallest.
  • Mark at 16 pxAt 16 px, use the Walnut tile everywhere, in browser tabs, app icons and single-color interfaces alike. It is the drawing players read as cards at that size. The one-color mark starts at 24 px.
  • Mark in printAt 5 mm or smaller, use the small-print master. 3.5 mm in 1-bit black is the smallest.
  • WordmarksChecked at 24 px tall. Below that, use the mark alone.

10

Imagery from real tables

Pictures show where Commander is played: someone's table, mid-game. Until the first real shoot, the book shows a table set from real things only.

The shot list

  • The pod, from aboveFour decks around a playmat, the way a player photographs their board.
  • Hands mid-gameShuffling, fanning a hand, turning a land sideways. Faces are optional.
  • The shelfDeck boxes in a row with their labels showing.
  • Store nightA Commander night at a local game store, tables full.

How it is shot

  • Overhead, or from the next seatFrame it tight enough that the cards read and loose enough that it is clearly someone's table.
  • Window light or warm tungstenShoot it like a phone photo, with a little grain and the real clutter left in.
  • True colorUse no tint and no filter, so card colors read as they do at the table.
  • Credit and consentEvery photograph credits who took it. Anyone recognizable is asked first.

Never

  • Stock photos of gamersThey are posed and lit, at a table nobody plays at.
  • Generated imagesOf any kind, anywhere.
  • Staged product rendersShow goods on a real shelf.
  • Glow, neon or lens flareNothing on the table glows.
  • Fantasy art as decorationCard art appears only as the card.

Six pieces, drawn from the current colors, type and mark. Each opens with a question and ends with the player deciding.

A guide page

It sits on the sheet, in light, with the question row, the byline, card rows with real keys and card images, the answer on the band, a player's take, and the way to tell us we're wrong.

Can my Atraxa deck run Boros Charm?

Renplays Atraxa superfriends

  • 1Boros CharmNo. Atraxa's color identity is white, blue, black and green, and Boros Charm has a red mana symbol.Color identity counts every mana symbol in a card's cost and rules text, and every card in the deck must fit inside the commander's.See CR903.4See CR903.5cWR

In my Atraxa deck I run Swords to Plowshares where you wanted Boros Charm. Your pod may like something else in that slot.

12

Accessibility

  • Contrast in both themesText at 4.5:1 or better and rules at 3:1 or better, on every allowed pairing, on the sheet and on the table. The 99 column is decoration and still reads at 4.5:1 or better.
  • Color is never the only signalKeys carry their letter, a state carries a word, and Ink text stays readable on both bands in grayscale.
  • Faces that separate I, l, 1, O and 0Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Mono draw them apart, in the 99 column and in every count.
  • Nothing you read under 12 pxLabels are the smallest text, at 13 / 18.
  • Focus is always visibleFocus shows as a 2 px outline in the text color, 2 px off the element.
  • Both themes are designedLight and dark follow the system setting, and each is drawn on its own.
  • Grayscale and 1-bit printThe wordmark, the keys and the label read from a home black-and-white printer at 25 mm.
  • The newcomer testNotes use a term, then make it plain in the same sentence.

Still open

Nothing here is approved yet. These are the brand calls and checks still waiting.

  • The words in Jaime's voiceThe opening story is written in Jaime's first person. He approves or rewrites it.
  • The first photo shootIt needs a real table with real decks: the pod from above, hands mid-game, the shelf and a store night. Every photo is credited and taken with consent. Jaime's own table is the first candidate.
  • The lettering commissionOne designer refines the mark, the Walnut tile and the wordmarks together, before the wordmarks are used in public. The brief asks for a hand-drawn 16 px version of the tile.
  • The player panelsPersona tests 1, 4, 7 and 11 need five real players each. For test 7 they see the Walnut tile at 16 and 32 px and the one-color mark at 32 px among other tab icons, before the lettering is signed off. Every panel so far used stand-ins, not players.
  • Real bylinesSam and Ren are samples. Guides publish only when a real player signs them.

Measurements behind the mark

Chosen by blind panels on November 14, 2026 (D-70, then D-72 for the 16 px fittings and D-74 for the tile's lines). Every panelist was a stand-in: a fresh AI model instance given a reader profile, not a real person.

Panel 1, four panelists, saw seven candidates beside the previous mark. At 32 px the played overlap was named as cards by 4 of 4, the only candidate to do so; at 16 px it drew 2 of 4.

Panels 2 and 3 used six unprimed panelists each: four as ordinary web users and two as people who play card and board games, with Magic never named. They saw eight 16 px fittings across the two panels, against a rule written before the results: cards as the first guess from at least 4 of 6, and at most one device, help, battery, folder, copy or lock guess. Every fitting failed. In panel 2 the rounded corners turned 7 px cards into circles, and the best new drawing reached 1 of 6. Panel 3 redrew the corners square, and the best reached 2 of 6: the two game players named cards, and the other four said two overlapping squares. The front-frame fitting shipped from panel 3 as an interim.

Panel 4 changed the reader, under a rule written before any panel 4 drawing or result. Persona test 7 defines the mark's reader as a Commander player, and ship review 5 asked for a panel drawn from Theo's and Maya's profiles, so panels 2 and 3 had gated on a stricter reader than the book's own test. Panel 4 used six panelists framed as people who play Commander most weeks, told nothing about cards, tapping, Magic icons or the brand, plus three non-players whose answers were reported but did not decide. They saw five new 16 px fittings and the panel 3 fitting as a control. The rule: at least 4 of 6 players name cards first, with at most one device, screen, help, battery, folder, copy, lock, coin, picture-in-picture or cast guess.

The color tile was named as cards first by 6 of 6 players and 3 of 3 non-players, with no wrong-family guess; two non-players added windows or tiles as a second guess. The one-color fitting with both cards solid was named as cards by 6 of 6 players and 0 of 3 non-players, with no wrong-family guess.

The Commander framing lifts every drawing: the panel 3 control drew 5 of 6 players but 0 of 3 non-players, and three panelists read it as a screen or window. The non-player column therefore separates the drawings, and only the color tile wins it. The tile ships for tabs and app icons, the one-color fitting for one-ink uses, and the front-frame fitting is retired. Ship review 7 then found the one-color 16 px fitting closest in silhouette to a devices icon among the neighbors, while the tile read as cards, so the one-color fitting was retired at 16 px too (D-76): at 16 px the tile is the only drawing, and one-color use starts at 24 px.

Panel 5 followed ship review 6, which read the color tile at 16 to 32 px as a four-pane window: its dark text-box lines ran from edge to edge and cut each card in two. Under a rule written before any panel 5 drawing, the same reader profiles as panel 4 saw three redrawn tiles and the shipped tile as a control, at 16 and 32 px, and window, layout, grid, pane, mosaic and dashboard guesses now counted as wrong. All three redrawn tiles were named as cards first by 6 of 6 players and 3 of 3 non-players at both sizes, with no wrong guess. The shipped tile drew "tiled windows", "window tiles" and "card grid layout": 5 of 6 players with one wrong guess at 16 px, and 1 of 3 non-players with two wrong guesses at 32 px. The tie went to the tile whose lines are a mid tone and stop short of the edge on both cards, with the front card's line on its left third, because it keeps the master's text-box line on both cards.

Overlap with common interface icons, 0 to 1, lower is more distinct, 0.80 or less passes. Filled outline fills both shapes and fits them to one box. Lines kept compares the drawings as rendered, holes and inner lines included, so a mark that draws panes meets a layout or window icon on equal terms. Each range runs over the drawn master, the one-color 16, 24, 32 and 48 px fittings, and the two cards of the 16 and 32 px Walnut tile. The tile itself is a plain rounded square, the shape every app icon shares, so only what sits on it is measured. Picture-in-picture, cast, screen share and orientation toggles were added after ship review 5, and layout, grid and window icons after ship review 6. The previous mark is shown for comparison.

Overlap scores alone do not show a pane reading, so the build also counts the separate light areas the tile's lines cut its two cards into: 2 at 16 px and 2 at 32 px. Two means two whole cards; four means the cards read as panes.

Pixel fittings, one color: 24 px, 10 by 14 with a 1 px gap; 32 px, 14 by 20 with a 2 px gap; 48 px, 22 by 31 with a 2 px gap; the line is 1 px at every size. Walnut tile, for favicons and app icons: at 16 px, a Walnut square with cut corners, upright card 7 by 10 and front card 10 by 7, each a Card Stock face inside a 1 px Ink border, the front card's border lying straight on the upright card's face. Each card's line is 1 px of Walnut Rule (#917F6A) with one Card Stock pixel between each end and the border; the front card's line sits on its left third, column 3 of 10 at 16 px, 4 of 14 at 24, 7 of 20 at 32 and 11 of 31 at 48. App icons draw the line the same way. 24 and 32 px follow the same rule with the one-color fittings' card sizes, and 48 px is drawn by it without a panel test. A 1 px ring in Walnut's border color (#917F6A, 4.29:1 on Walnut) runs round the tile's edge, because plain Walnut vanishes on a Walnut page and nearly vanishes on dark tab strips. App icons at 180 and 512 px use the drawn master in the same colors on full-bleed Walnut. Drawn master: a 100-unit square, cards 50 by 70, gap 4 units, split 1.8. Small-print and wordmark master: gap 5.2, split 2.6, so both hold at 3.5 mm and in a wordmark 32 px tall.
